references.text: In the conversation on the road to Emmaus, the disciples recount the women's testimony that they did not find Jesus' body: [ref:Luk 24:23|Luke 24:23] confirms that they "did not find his body" – a direct reference to the event at the tomb.
Joseph of Arimathea laid Jesus' body in a carved tomb ([ref:Luk 23:53|Luke 23:53]). The fact that the women now do not find the body shows that the known and sealed tomb was empty.
In [ref:Mark 16:5-6|Mark 16:5-6], the women enter the tomb and find it empty, and an angel tells them that Jesus has risen. The parallel account confirms the empty tomb.
Also in [ref:Matt 28:5-6|Matthew 28:5-6], the women discover that Jesus' body is not there, and the angel says "He is not here, for he has risen." This parallels the empty tomb in Luke.

In [ref:Joh 20:1-2|John 20:1-2], Mary Magdalene finds the stone rolled away and concludes that the Lord's body is gone. John's account confirms that the tomb was empty, consistent with Luke's testimony.
In [ref:Joh 20:6-7|John 20:6-7], Peter enters the tomb and finds only the linen cloths, but no body. This underscores the same point as Luke 24:3 – Jesus' body was gone.

Peter proclaims in his Pentecost sermon that Christ "was not abandoned to the realm of the dead, nor did his body see decay" ([ref:Apg 2:31|Acts 2:31]). The empty tomb is a central proof of the resurrection that Peter testifies to.

Paul proclaims in [ref:Apg 13:29-30|Acts 13:29-30] that Jesus was laid in a tomb, but that God raised him from the dead. The empty tomb – that the body was not found – is the premise for the proclamation of the resurrection.
